earlier_scan.source_named: Volker, Craig Alan. 1998. The Nalik Language of New Ireland, Papua New Guinea. New York: Peter Lang.
earlier_scan.note: Full grammar (also Volker 1994 PhD thesis) exists in print; no open-access copy found

sources.citation: Beaumont, C. H. 1972. New Ireland languages: a review. In Papers in Linguistics of Melanesia No. 3, 1-41. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics A-35. DOI 10.15144/PL-A35.1
sources.note: §1.4 Phonology is a survey of segment inventories reported for New Ireland languages (Nalik has f, z, etc.); no word on stress or accent anywhere in the paper.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Nalik language' (accessed 2026-09-17); Glottolog 5.x languoid page nali1244
sources.note: Wikipedia phonology section (consonants, vowels, diphthongs, dialectal lenition) says nothing about stress; cites Beaumont 1972, Volker 1994, Volker 1998. Glottolog lists only Ross 1988/1994 and Ethnologue on the page; alternative names Fesoa, Fessoa, Lugagon.

sources.citation: Volker, Craig Alan. 2025. The convergence of Nalik with Tok Pisin: Two languages becoming one linguistic repertoire. In Nataliya Levkovych, Julia Nintemann & Maike Vorholt (eds), Exploring Structures in Languages and Language Contact, 95-1xx. Berlin: De Gruyter. DOI 10.1515/9783111496436-005 (open access, CC BY-NC-ND)
sources.note: §3 Phonology (pp. 98-101) covers consonant inventory (Table 2, from Volker 1998), f/v s/z p/w t/r k/x alternations, loss of /ɣ/, and phonemic vowel length (laraf vs laraaf). No mention of stress or accent. States 'A basic overview of Nalik phonology has been described in Volker (1998)'.

sources.citation: Mazzitelli, Lidia Federica. 2020. Documentation of Lakurumau: Making the case for one more language in Papua New Guinea. Language Documentation & Conservation 14: 215-237.http://hdl.handle.net/10125/24922
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Silent on stress; cites Volker 1998 for Nalik subject markers and nominalizers; identifies Lakurumau (the Nalik-Kara 'transitional' variety) as a separate language.

sources.citation: Dryer, Matthew S. 2012. A grammatical description of Kara-Lemakot. Canberra: Asia-Pacific Linguistics.http://hdl.handle.net/1885/10703
sources.note: Gives a stress rule for KARA (kara1486), not Nalik: last /a:/ stressed, else last closed syllable, else initial. Nalik is cited only for morphosyntax (Volker 1998). Not usable for Nalik.

sources.citation: Volker, Craig. 1996. A Lingmaam 1: A Ikakating wan a ling a Nalik / Nalik Dictionary Project 1: Nalik Mathematics. Bulletin of Gifu College of Education (聖徳学園岐阜教育大学紀要) 32: 1-33.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: No stress rule. Gives the Nalik orthography (Fig. 1, p. 3) and, p. 10, says two sacred numerals carry marked intonation and are 'the only recorded instances of individual words in Nalik requiring obligatory tone' (i.e., no lexical tone otherwise). Nothing on stress placement.

sources.citation: Volker, Craig. 1996. Variation in Nalik grammar. In John Lynch & Fa'afo Pat (eds), Oceanic Studies: Proceedings of the First International Conference on Oceanic Linguistics, 451-462. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics C-133. DOI 10.15144/PL-C133.451
sources.note: Silent; morphosyntactic variation only. Names four geographic dialects (Northern East Coast, Southern East Coast, West Coast, Laefu) plus Nalik-Kara transitional dialects excluded from the data.

sources.citation: Ross, Malcolm D. 1988. Proto Oceanic and the Austronesian languages of Western Melanesia. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics C-98. DOI 10.15144/PL-C98
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL6201.R67 1988)
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL6201 .R67 1988
sources.note: 95 mentions of Nalik (subgrouping, sound changes, pronouns) but no stress statement for Nalik; the only stress remarks concern Ali and Huon Gulf (Hote/Buang) languages.

sources.citation: Beaumont, C. H. 1976. Austronesian languages: New Ireland. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea Area Languages and Language Study, vol. 2: Austronesian languages, 387-397. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics C-39. DOI 10.15144/PL-C39.387
sources.note: Silent; comparative sound correspondences only (Nalik reflexes of *p, *q, etc.).
